A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same preference-optimized watermark-evasion study. Their complete main texts, figures, tables, equations, and appendices support comparison, and the original algorithm and experiments can be matched across the restructuring.

before.justification: v1 reports original attack-training experiments, evasion and text-quality measurements, ablations, and generated-text examples in Section 5 and the appendix.

after.justification: v2 retains the original empirical results and adds watermark evaluations, GPT-4o comparisons, and analyses of paraphrased text in Appendices A.4–A.7.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 retains surrogate-key generation, repeated paraphrasing, quality-and-detection filtering, preference pairing, and DPO optimization. The revised pseudocode is equivalent. Training a Qwen2.5-3b paraphraser against Unigram applies the existing procedure to another watermark without introducing a method component.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates Exp, Dist-Shift, Binary, and Inverse. v2 adds SynthID, Unigram, and SIR evaluations, including training against Unigram, substantially expanding the watermark-generation conditions tested. KGW corresponds to the retained Dist-Shift scheme. The underlying task remains text generation and paraphrasing.

E2.justification: v2 adds GPT-4o as an evaluated paraphrasing comparator in Figure 7 and the subsequent text analyses; v1's closed-model comparator was GPT3.5. The original DIPPER, translation, word-perturbation, and open-model baseline families remain, so this is a limited extension of the comparator set.

E3.justification: The added appendix evaluation uses a 256-token limit and GPT-4o-mini as quality judge, while the original evaluation retains its existing settings and Llama3-8B judge. Appendix A.7 additionally evaluates n-gram overlap and normalized token edit distance. These are new evaluation protocols, not demonstrated changes to the original experiments.

E4.justification: Appendices A.5–A.7 add distributions of text lengths, quality scores, and watermark scores, top-50-token comparisons, and n-gram/edit-distance analyses investigating attack behavior. The original model-size, adaptivity, FPR, watermark-bias, and example-based analyses remain; moving the FPR and bias studies into the appendix does not remove them.

E5.justification: v1 Figure 2 identifies its shaded bands as one standard deviation; v2 retains the bands but removes that explanation. The 95% confidence-interval description remains for the Qwen repetition experiment, moved from Figure 7 to Figure 6. No new repeated-run counts, seed reporting, or significance-testing procedures are documented.

E6.justification: v2 adds substantial results in Figures 7 and 9–15, including watermark-specific GPT-4o trade-offs and lower n-gram overlap after optimization. Figure 7 retains GPT-4o on the SIR and KGW Pareto fronts. Original results such as Figure 3 and the quality table remain numerically unchanged. However, v2 Table 4 retains v1 Table 3's values while reversing their quality/evasion labels, creating inconsistent metric assignments.

T1.justification: Section 3 changes the stated attacker assumption from black-box API access to no-box access without provider watermarked training samples. Appendix A.7 introduces mathematical definitions for the newly evaluated overlap and edit-distance ratios. The original robustness inequality and optimization objective retain their substance, and no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The central claim of inexpensive, transferable adaptive evasion remains. v2's contribution statement qualifies broad superiority as Pareto optimality above 90% evasion, explicitly acknowledging GPT-4o's quality advantage on some Pareto fronts. It also emphasizes success under the more restrictive no-box threat model and adds public paraphraser release as a contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations involving token-sequence avoidance, lexical substitutions, and learned edit distance, plus an interpretation of shorter outputs as a consequence of not penalizing brevity. It explicitly acknowledges imperfect alignment between LLM judges and human judgment and discusses restrictions of closed-model attacks. These substantially expand v1's mechanism discussion and applicability qualifications.

D1.justification: v2 newly documents the 296-prompt evaluation set and its non-overlap with the retained 1,000-prompt training set, the MarkLLM implementation, and the GPT-4o version used. It changes a promised code/model release to a reported paraphraser release at a new repository location. The original hardware, prompting, optimizer, and LoRA details remain.

R1.justification: v2 substantively positions the work against Jovanovic and Pang's sample-dependent attacks and Zhang's impossibility/random-walk setting, emphasizing inexpensive no-box optimization. It also adds references for SynthID, Unigram, SIR, MarkLLM, and AutoPrompt, while removing Nicks and Uchida citations. The revised distinctions materially expand the account of how this work differs from prior research.

P1.justification: The abstract, contributions, threat model, and discussion are extensively revised. Related Work moves before the method, contributions become integrated introductory prose, and the FPR and bias discussions move into a substantially reorganized appendix. The title is shortened and terminology is standardized throughout.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from a single-column preprint to a two-column proceedings layout. v2 adds a workflow schematic and multiple analytical figures, resizes and relocates retained plots, changes Table 2 from stacked examples to three columns, and splits the bias table's paired values into labeled subcolumns. These are substantial visual and display changes.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the evidence beyond v1's four-watermark evaluation through three additional watermark schemes, GPT-4o comparisons, a different quality judge, and direct textual analyses in Appendices A.4–A.7. Clearer training/evaluation documentation and explicit judge limitations also improve assessability. New reporting defects, including reversed Table 4 headings, conflicting overlap definitions in Equation 3 and Figure 15, and Figure 13's caption/legend mismatch, weaken specific details. Nevertheless, the broader comparative evidence and deeper analysis provide a substantial net quality improvement.
